articles.title: Politics awakens?
articles.content: THE long, hard summer is coming to an end, and with it, politics seems to be awakening from its hibernation. It may partly have been the end of the summer holiday at parliament, but for once, the politicians are not simply using the new session to blindly vote for legislation. The rundown halls of the big building on Constitution Avenue are witnessing some politicking too, as party delegations connect for discussions and strategising. Even Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who has spent the past two years playing hard to get, seems to be considering a ‘date’. The PPP, too, is, for once, doing more than paying lip service to the idea of sitting together. The rains have rejuvenated far more than the greenery in the capital. But even the parliamentarians could not take attention away from their neighbours next door. After months of petitions and chatter about Imran Khan’s health, the Supreme Court alsoheld a hearing on the matter. Perhaps this was due to the‘alarming’ report on his medical well-beingwhich made its way to the judges. It is still a bit unclear who ordered it and why but the court asked for a health check-up and a hospital stay for the former prime minister. What followed the court’s order was pandemonium. After all, Khan has been locked up and has been out of sight (but not out of mind), since he wasarrested before the election. A court order which allowed him to meet his family, consult his doctors and stay in hospital seemed impossible concessions, considering the non-stop messaging about how Khan was not acceptable to those who matter. In this land, where conspiracies rule the roost and even prove to be true at times, everyone, including the PTI, thought something was up. So did the government. Indeed, it seemed the government took a page out of the PTI’s book — in which there is more contradiction than agreement. The government was proved right as the order was not implemented the way many assumed — Khantook a road trip to hospital and then back to Adiala. But it was not the hospital the court had ordered nor did he get to consult his own doctor. So, what happened and what went wrong? Co-option cannot happen at the level of high politics without also including the people. After all, our courts do not give orders which will not be implemented. That really isn’t how Constitution Avenue works. No wonder some went so far as to think that the hearing came after some behind-the-scenes understanding. And of course, those who believe such fairy-tales then also argued that, at the last minute, someone, somewhere changed their mind. The finger is being pointed at the government, for it has the most to lose from any ‘relief’ given to the PTI and its leader. But it is worth asking if the PML-N component in Islamabad or Lahore has the power or the space to make such decisions. After all, the manner in which Pakistan is being run, the decision to take Khan to hospital and meet his family could not have been lightly taken or at any unimportant level. And so, if it was scuttled, it was done by someone as powerful as the one who made the original decision. If we allow for these assumptions, does it mean that there is some disagreement at the top about how to treat the PTI? The answer to this question will be evident once the court hears the PTI’s contempt of court petition and says something about it. The party has alreadyapproached the courtcomplaining that the latter’s orders were not implemented. That the petition names government ministers other than Mohsin Naqvi is worth noting. As an aside, it is interesting that the time period from Nawaz Sharif’sdisqualificationin the summer of 2017 to thevote of no-confidencein April 2022 is similar to the period from the VONC to the present. A little short of five years. Relief from imprisonment doesn’t necessarily mean the end of all troubles but it does indicate that there is some softening of attitudes, whatever the reason. But to repeat, all of this will become a little clearer if and when the Supreme Court gets around to dealing with the petition. There is a larger issue here that escapes the attention of those who focus on high politics in Islamabad. And that is of the people, whose support has turned Imran Khan into the force he is. Large parts of this support is linked to the anger the people feel towards the state’s policies of high taxes, an affordability crisis, the lack of security and the absence of economic opportunities. The list may be longer. This anger is why, despite the utter lack of competence displayed by the PTI and the imprisonment of Khan, his popularity has not faded. For people need hope and they have pinned this hope on the cricketer-turned-politician. If he and his party now reach an understanding with the establishment, as did Nawaz Sharif and the PML-N some years back, what will the people do? This is not a question to be ignored. It is illogical to assume that the anger will dissipate just because Khan is released — even if he returns to power — if the crises facing the populace are not addressed. People will simply dump Khan the way some of them ditched Nawaz Sharif. Will they then still believe in mainstream politics or turn to more extreme options? Indeed, it is important to understand that co-option cannot happen at the level of high politics without also including the people. Those who think this is possible need to pay a little more attention to what is happening in Balochistan. Parliamentary politics or political parties can be effective only as long as they are linked to and carry the people along. The PTI and those engaging the party should remember this.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: March with hope, but verify
articles.content: IT’S always uplifting to be hopeful, more so when the young ones give us an elusive glimpse into their hope. But youth is not a worldview or an ideology. Young ones have handed us despair too. They’re on the march against America’s alliance with Zionism. But they’re also part of the 90 per cent Israelis who advocate genocide in Palestine. Closer to home, the RSS cultivates youth as did the Nazis. To belong to the young communist league in the USSR was to embody the future of a dream that faded too soon. Young activists invoke mixed responses in South Asia where politics has suspended its left-right discourse for something called centrist and pragmatic politics. Pragmatism is too often a ruse for putting lipstick on the pig. The posture is worrisome but there are other reasons to be prepared for a determined pushback from the state if the wayward rulers with their monopoly over the means of coercion feel truly threatened, say, by the youth as glimpsed partly inDelhi’s Cockroach event. Consider the facts carefully. Twelve Latin American countries have recently veered to the right, reversing the region’s previous ‘pink tide’ of left-leaning governments. A wave of election cycles has fundamentally altered the region’s political landscape. Notable among the renegades are Colombia, Peru, Argentina, El Salvador, Chile, Ecuador, Bolivia, Panama, Costa Rica, Honduras and Paraguay. Factors are not too different from South Asia’s. High inflation, social inequality, corruption and post-pandemic economic stagnation are listed as driving the massive anti-incumbent sentiment. The ‘Trump Effect’ is cited as a factor even if the enduring impression in Europe and Asia is of the US being evicted from its comfort zone in the oil-rich Gulf. Many leaders in Latin America are actively copying the ‘Bukele model’ of mass incarceration and hard-line security borrowed from the El Salvadoran dictator. South Asia has not remained untouched. The deposed leader of one country is languishing in jail and that of another country is a fugitive from those who drove her from office with street power. The right-wing Indian prime minister has coined a new description for what could be his next target — the thinking youth. So, who are the “dimaghi Naxals” Modi has warned the country about? Che Guevara and John Keats lived a century apart but they may have offered a likely pointer to who exactly could be in Narendra Modi’s crosshairs. “If you tremble with indignation at every injustice then you are a comrade of mine,” said Che. “Where but to think is to be full of sorrow,” mused Keats, describing the human condition to a bohemian nightingale. Has the new generation found the courage and the commitment to face the consequences of a massive pushback? Before joining the jubilant crowds at theresignationof Modi’s powerful education minister whose removal the Cockroach protesters had sought, it would do no harm to remember that Indira Gandhi was similarly forced to remove two of her chief ministers — Chimanbhai Patel in Gujarat and Abdul Ghafoor in Bihar — in the run-up to the Emergency. With her back to the wall after a court verdict sought her removal from power, she went for the trigger and jailed her opponents. Mrs Gandhi was essentially a democrat, not the best in the world but also not the worst. There was no other valid reason for her to hold elections after having vanquished the violent surge against her. How can we know that Modi would not consider harsher measures should things come to the crunch? The political circumstances seem a lot more fraught today than they were in 1975 on the eve of the Emergency. A commission of inquiry probed Indira Gandhi’s excesses following her defeat in the 1977 elections (which she had called in the alleged belief she would sweep the polls). Whatever the Shah Commission found on her was not enough to send her for more than a night’s stay in Tihar Jail. But look at the list of excesses called out by Modi’s opponents today. Moreover, there are deeply entrenched domestic and foreign interest groups who dread the Modi government losing power. What would become of the TV channels and their ace anchors that have become a platform for hate speech and servitude to the government? What would become of the temple heist probe? At an international level, what would become of the $250 million corruption charge slammed on Gautam Adani and the opposition’s claim that after Donald Trump took office, the US Justice Department contrived to drop the cases. This reversal allegedly came after Adani hired a personal lawyer of Trump (Robert J. Giuffra Jr) and extended an unusual offer to invest $10 billion into the American economy to create 15,000 jobs. Opposition leaders claim Modi actively “covered up” this corporate corruption during high-level US diplomatic meetings. What would be Israel’s reaction should the Modi government ever be stuck in the political doldrums? The entire Western world rose up in arms against Indira Gandhi’s Emergency not least because she was identified as a Soviet ally. Today, the West is silent over a raging genocide in Gaza; how would it find the courage to speak for Indian democracy, particularly when the Modi government is “doing the job” for them? Therefore, the question is, has the new generation found the courage and the commitment to face the consequences of a massive pushback? Pakistan, in India’s neighbourhood, has seen momentous changes, including coups as well as the eviction of usurpers. But it is equally a fact that when Ziaul Haq hanged an elected prime minister, there wasn’t the mass upheaval against his tormentors that ZAB had hoped for. Tariq Ali underscores the irony in his playThe Leopard and The Fox. While localised street clashes occurred in places like Rawalpindi, Lahore and Sindh, protests against Bhutto’s hanging remained fragmented. Therefore, when the “dimaghi Naxals” and assorted “cockroaches” ponder their next brave moves, they might want to blend with their abiding hopes a dose of prescribed preparedness. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: KPT expressway
articles.content: ALL over the world, especially in the Global North, elevated expressways and flyovers are no longer built. Not only that, those which were built in the last century are being demolished. The space they vacate is being turned into public spaces (such as parks and sports facilities) for the benefit of city residents, especially the youth. These demolitions and conversions are seen in the US, Europe and the UK. Even in South Korea, over 13 flyovers are being replaced by recreational spaces. Also cities no longer tolerate polluting expressways through their cultural and or city centres. They bypass them. This is a concept well-understood by our planners who have designed and implemented bypasses for many Pakistan’s cities but in many cases, due to real estate and other construction, these bypasses no longer act as such and do not have any relationship in the planning process to our cultural heritage. A very important road is now being envisaged for Karachi from the KPT to Shahrah-i-Bhutto. This is because the Karachi Port generates a volume of traffic that the city’s infrastructure cannot handle. Due to this reality, there are huge traffic jams at the exit points to the city, which also creates congestion in other parts of the city. These traffic jams, especially at the exit points and the Karachi Port Trust, can last for hours, causing economic loss to not just KPT but to the entire country. Given these conditions, Karachi’s civic agencies have decided to build a road that connects KPT to Shahrah-i-Bhutto, thus creating an additional exit to the city to solve this very serious problem. It is true that port-related traffic needs an additional outlet from KPT, since all outlets are heavily congested and are the cause of major traffic jams at the outlets where trucks travelling to the north have to wait for hours to move. However, the proposal, if implemented, will ruin the city aesthetically and environmentally. No city in the world today is likely to implement such a proposal. The journey of this road will be through the Mai Kolachi bypass, which passes through an open area of 1,400 acres. A KPT housing colony was supposed to be constructed here but was stopped through a court order following citizens’ objection. The expressway is bound to threaten Karachi’s ecology. This area can be developed as an urban forest and a playground for young sportsmen and can be an important lung for the city, which has few open spaces and almost no sports facilities. This road will turn the area into a noisy, polluted zone, and during the monsoon season, the winds from the sea will carry both the noise and the fumes of the traffic to the city centre. The chief minister’s office will also be affected by it. Following this, the road will also pass through Defence Society. Here its journey will be through Sunset Boulevard, one of the most elite areas of the city. This journey will also be mostly elevated. This port-related traffic, which will consist mostly of heavy trailers, will adversely affect the privacy of the residents, and create noise and pollution, including in its construction phase. Given these conditions it will be difficult for many residents to continue to live on Sunset Boulevard and the areas adjacent to it. The road will then pass through Qayyumabad and its adjoining low-income settlements. Their already fragile health will be further affected by the fumes and noise of the heavy traffic. Finally, the road will join up with Malir Expressway, which has already been considered an environmental disaster and which is said to have an adverse effect on the ecology of the Malir area. Given these conditions, the road will substantially increase pollution in the Malir corridor. The Malir corridor was planned to be banned for rickshaws and motorcycles for environmental and safety reasons, and with this road there will be increased environmental hazards and the original purpose of the Malir corridor will be negated. Given what has been said about it, it is necessary to find another solution which does not pass through the city and does not create further environmental stress for Karachi. One option is to take a road from KPT to behind Machhar Colony and to join it at some point with M-9. It might cost more but it will be worth it. Let us spend public funds judiciously. It is encouraging to see that the government agencies are desirous of engaging the citizens of Karachi in taking this important decision. It is hoped that this will happen for all other important projects as well and that the citizens’ concerns will be addressed.
articles.author: Arif Hasan

articles.title: UNSC reforms
articles.content: THE UN system, established after 1945, reflected the realities of a Hobbesian world, in which the victors’ justice was codified in the UN Charter that gave the five major World War II victors the power to keep their interests protected and their rivalries ring-fenced in a veto cage. Though the present UN Charter defines the legality of war and the territorial rights of each member state through Article 2(4), there is no check or meaningful cost on the breach of the same article by veto-wielding powers of the P5. The result is the inability of the UN General Assembly and UN Security Council to prevent genocide and violation of sovereign states’ territorial integrity. The Atlantic Charter that birthed Nato too suffered from the same anomalies of power politics. Nato, instead of the putative collective security under Article 5, was known more by its first secretary general Lord Ismay’s observation: “Nato was created to keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.” The UN system and UNSC are beset with the same anomalies. Despite the best intentions and exertions of the 10 non-permanent member states, the five permanent veto-wielding states can stymie all efforts at peace enforcement. The veto-based system reflects power asymmetry, not the democratic acuity needed to prevent conflicts in a fragmented world. Democratic retreat in global politics appears in the form of unilateralism, tariff wars, de-globalisation and emasculation of institutions of economic cooperation (WTO). At a time when great power competition is redefining the rules of the game for the weak, the Kantian world is giving way to a Hobbesian one. In an environment when the weak fend for themselves and the UN Charter fails to prevent crimes against humanity, annexations and genocide, it makes little sense to add more layers of privilege to the UNSC. Reforms should aim to make it more democratic, inclusive and capable of increasing the cost of veto against genocide, crimes against humanity and violation of territorial integrity. UfC’s model provides an incremental approach. Without this, reforms cannot resolve peace and security issues. There are several groups peddling ideas for UNSC reform. One is the G4 Proposal(Brazil, Germany, India, Japan), which espouses the expansion of both permanent and non-permanent UNSC membership by granting permanent seats to G4 countries, allocating two permanent seats to Africa and increasing elected non-permanent seats. Another one is the African Group comprising 54 African Union member states. It is asking for two permanent seats with full prerogatives, including veto powers as they exist and five non-permanent seats in an expanded Council. The France-Mexico Initiative has called on P5 to voluntarily refrain from using veto in situations involving mass atrocities such as genocide, crimes against humanity and large-scale war crimes. The United for Peace (UfC) proposal led by Pakistan and supported by Italy, Mexico, Argentina, Canada and South Korea rejects any expansion of the permanent membership category, with or without veto powers. It advocates for expanding elected non-permanent seats through longer-term and re-electable membership. A cursory look at these proposals indicate that except for the UfC, the proposals do not address the core issue at the heart of the UNSC’s dysfunctionality — veto powers and the rest of the member states’ inability to confront the veto even when it’s used in pursuit of the P5’s geopolitical objectives that might run athwart international law, the notion of collective security and fidelity to Article 2(4). It is good to support the idea of geographical representation especially for African nations; however, the metamorphosis of victims into veto-wielding hegemons would exacerbate the present iniq-uity. The quest of individual countries for permanent seats has to be seen in the context of the broader aims of equitable representation, justice and efficacy of an expanded UNSC. The UfC’s is the only proposal that offers the UNSC’s expansion by increasing the number of non-permanent seats with a re-election provision and essentially freezing inequity by limiting permanent seats to the existing P5, besides enhancing regional representation from Africa, Asia-Pacific, West Asia and Latin America. The UfC model provides an incremental approach that can adapt to evolving geopolitical realities through periodic elections rather than permanent structural changes. Finally, due care should be taken to not enhance iniquity by adding more wannabes as permanent UNSC members. Countries like India, which are serial violators of the UNSC resolutions and have annexed disputed regions besides remaining outside UN-affiliated treaties like NPT and CTBT, certainly do not fit the bill as permanent UNSC members.
articles.author: Dr Raashid Wali Janjua

articles.title: Fixing agriculture
articles.content: PRIME Minister Shehbaz Sharif’srenewed pushto strengthen agricultural research, provide quality seeds to smallholders and medium-scale farmers, and improve crop estimate systems could help address some of the sector’s long-standing weaknesses in farm productivity. But good intentions alone are not enough. The real question is whether the government can turn his directives into a coherent policy and implement it effectively. That would require reforming federal and provincial agriculture policies, markets and institutions that determine what farmers produce, what they pay for inputs and what they earn. Above all, an agricultural policy must be responsive to the needs of small and medium-sized farmers rather than powerful lobbies. Take the example of the sugar sector. Policy has repeatedly been designed around the interests of millers, who have traditionally enjoyed political influence. Decisions on support prices, cane procurement, export, and other interventions aim to protect them. Cotton illustrates another failure of the agricultural system. Farmers often do not receive a fair share of the value generated by their crop, with middlemen and other parts of the supply chain capturing much of the margin. The result is reduced yields over the years. Improving farm productivity means little if farmers remain trapped in inefficient markets and weak bargaining arrangements. A serious agricultural reform programme must address these structural problems. Smallholders need easier and cheaper access to bank credit, fairly priced and reliable inputs, protection against adulterated pesticides and poor-quality fertiliser and certified, high-yielding and climate-resilient seeds. They also need better extension services that take modern farming techniques from research institutions to the field. Market reform is as important. Farmers should have greater direct access to efficient markets and buyers, instead of remaining dependent on middlemen. Better storage, grading, transport, digital market information and transparent price mechanisms can help reduce the gap between what consumers pay and what farmers receive. The proposed national system for estimating crop production is overdue. Reliable data is essential for planning imports, exports, storage and prices. But such a system will be useful only if its estimates are credible and produced through modern technology. The question, therefore, is not whether the PM’s intentions are honest. They are. The question is whether his government has what it takes to confront the entrenched interests that benefit from the system. Agricultural modernisation requires a comprehensive plan covering research, seeds, credit, inputs, extension, markets, water management and value chains, with the smallholder at its centre. It also requires political will to reform policies that currently favour powerful groups. Without these, no intervention will deliver the productive gains that farmers and the economy urgently need.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Secure identities
articles.content: THE common citizen’s interactions with the bureaucracy are rarely pleasant in Pakistan. But over the last 26 years, at least where securing identity documents is concerned, Nadra has attempted to streamline this process. The latest development in this regard is the move to make proof of life certificates required by pensioners free, and to expand the channels through which senior citizens can access the document. Seniors can now personally, or through an immediate family member, access the certificates through the PakID mobile app, eliminating the need for physical verification. Nadra also recently created the National Pensioners Register to help eliminate fraud, and streamline verification. Moreover, the authority has announced the launch of QR-based ID cards, which will replace chip-based cards. This should help reduce data entry errors. The creation of Nadra in 2000 resulted in the replacement of the old National Identity Cards — which were much easier to forge — with computerised IDs. Though the authority has achieved much over the decades, there is still room for improvement. For example, it has suffered major data breaches, which resulted in the sensitive information of millions of citizens being leaked to unscrupulous elements. Therefore, in the digital age, improved cybersecurity is essential for Nadra to protect the personal information of citizens. Those not entitled to CNICs — for instance, foreigners — are still able to secure the key document because of the presence of corrupt officials within the organisation. Hence, better internal oversight is needed; Nadra says it has introduced AI tools and iris scanning to identify ineligible individuals who have secured ID cards. Overcrowding and long queues at Nadra centres are another matter of concern for the public. Partly because of the large number of applicants, and partly due to bureaucratic lethargy and system breakdowns, applicants often have to queue up for hours to get their documents made. These processes need to be made faster and more efficient without compromising essential security checks, although the promotion of the Nadra app can perhaps help reduce the long lines at registration centres. Nadra needs to keep adapting to keep pace with the digital age, while also ensuring that citizens have a hassle-free experience when getting their documents made.
articles.author: Editorial
